# Negotiation Arena

Python harness for buyer agents in the Tacto negotiation challenge. It supports
local experiments, agent comparisons and execution of the live final. Hosted
profiles require explicit authorization.

## Start locally

You need Git, Python 3.12 and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/). After cloning this
repository, run:

```bash
cd starter-kit
uv sync --frozen --extra sim --group dev
uv run --frozen arena-harness doctor
uv run --frozen arena-harness run --agent baseline
```

The default runs three scripted simulator cases with no external Arena or model
calls. Results, journals and reports go to the ignored `.runs/` directory at the
repo root. Simulator scores help compare local behavior; they do not predict
performance against live suppliers.

## Repository structure

| Location | Purpose |
|---|---|
| [`starter-kit/agents/`](starter-kit/agents/) | Agent implementations and a copyable `example.py` |
| [`starter-kit/configs/`](starter-kit/configs/) | Experiment configuration: agent, parameters, model and limits; no keys |
| [`starter-kit/arena_kit/harness/`](starter-kit/arena_kit/harness/) | API communication, execution, recovery and reporting |
| [`starter-kit/arena_kit/`](starter-kit/arena_kit/) | Existing cost calculation, data access, document parsing and simulator |
| [`starter-kit/tests/`](starter-kit/tests/) | Local tests; hosted tests require explicit selection |
| [`brief/`](brief/) | Official challenge, API and submission requirements |
| [`data/`](data/) | Official procurement data, facts, SQLite, contracts and notes |
| [`example_inputs/`](example_inputs/) | Recorded simulator inputs and attachments for inspection |
| `.runs/` (ignored) | Local run state and exports |

There is one Python project, with its `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock` in
`starter-kit/`. Run Python commands there. New agent implementations belong in
`starter-kit/agents/`; `starter-kit/arena_kit/agents/` contains the original
starter examples, exposed through harness adapters.

## Development

Follow the [Python workspace guide](starter-kit/README.md) to add an agent and
configuration. Keep each approach in its own agent/config pair, run it locally,
and compare matching cases and data versions using `arena-harness compare`.
Changes go through a feature branch and pull request; commit agent code and
configuration so runs can be reproduced. Do not commit keys, `.env` or run state.

The harness permits one run per OS user and machine. Coordinate hosted runs
across machines using the same Arena key and quota. The original `arena`
CLI has separate execution and configuration; use `arena-harness` for
experiments and final execution.

## Hosted runs and the final

[HARNESS.md](starter-kit/HARNESS.md) documents the full CLI, agent interface,
model limits, final start and recovery. Hosted sessions require `--allow-arena`;
remote models separately require `--allow-model` and configured call/output
limits. Keys come from `ARENA_API_KEY` and `LLM_API_KEY` in the environment.
Having a key does not activate a hosted profile, and the harness does not load
`.env` automatically.

Before the final, commit the selected agent, configuration and data, check a
clean checkout and use `--commit` with the full HEAD SHA. Start before the first
wave and follow the [final/recovery instructions](starter-kit/HARNESS.md#final-and-recovery).
The final runs without confirmation dialogs. Passing local tests does not
validate the live connection; perform a hosted smoke test only after explicit
authorization.

- [Data package](data/README.md)
- [Original starter library examples and MCP setup](starter-kit/REFERENCE.md)

Findings from practice back-office logs and traces (night of 2026-10-10/11, see starter-kit/EVALUATION.md):
- RFQ: a bidder shown a *much lower* rival quote (rival_quote claim, an `offer:` ID) gives half the step at
  once ("we will come back to you on price") and next round moves to max(our ask, its floor). Citing the
  rival in the opening lifted P05 0.67 -> 0.82 (baa6c1f). Holding our ask in the "come back" round made the
  cheapest bidder withdraw in 2/2 runs -> rejected.
- Suppliers issue final offers at a nearly fixed round per supplier (1-6); the round-1 counter sets most of
  the outcome. No reciprocity: our larger concessions did not draw larger supplier moves.
- Sometimes the engine decides "final_offer" and then withdraws instead (P02 2/8 recent runs) - stochastic.
- Sold-out (full_order_book) suppliers price shorter lead time at 0.2-0.5 %/day (2a97328, 0.722 run).
- Index-fall claims to forward-hedged suppliers: "not our reality", yet a lower first counter (73dfaa8).
- price_history and should_cost never move a price; later-round messages with a fresh checked argument
  drew larger supplier moves (round 2 median 1.08 % vs 0.31 %).
- RFQ quote PDF downloads time out behind other bidders' messages (arena serves a session serially);
  fixed in 2631678 (latest readable quote documents an offer).
- Analysis tooling: scratchpad trace.py / fetchall.py pull /v1/sessions/{sid} and /backoffice (no quota).

Related: [[recursive-improvement-loop]], [[no-overfitting]], [[arena-final-context]]

Use the current [official submission requirements](../brief/submission.md).
Load the official Sunday release into `data/release-sunday/`; overlapping fact
IDs are rejected. Commit the selected code, agent, configuration and data before
the freeze. Ensure the machine stays awake and connected. Only one machine per
Arena key should run live: the lock covers one OS user on one machine and does
not coordinate execution across different computers. The legacy `arena` CLI is
independent of this lock; use `arena-harness` for experiments and the final.

```bash

uv run arena-harness run --profile final --config configs/final.toml \
  --allow-arena --allow-model --commit FULL_HEAD_SHA
```

large enough for the final. The code must be clean and `--commit` must match HEAD.
Startup permission is persisted: the runner polls five waves and resumes without
confirmation dialogs. It never requests leaderboard/events/results/backoffice.
The final uses server deadlines, up to ten sessions, nine requests/second and
concurrent supplier requests. Quotes and worker decisions have bounded processing
budgets. Near the wave cap it closes conservatively.

The supervisor holds a per-user OS lock outside the checkout (under
`$XDG_STATE_HOME/arena-harness`, or `~/.local/state/arena-harness`) and restarts a
crashed engine at most three times. The engine inherits the lock descriptor, so
killing only the supervisor does not permit a competing run. Every POST is
journaled before sending; retries use its original `X-Move-Id`. Never delete a run
journal to retry a final case. Resume requires unchanged commit, code, agent and
data, plus the original Arena key. Agent fingerprints cover the team `agents/`
tree, including imported helpers; dependency fingerprints cover `pyproject.toml`
and `uv.lock`. Existing journals remain reportable, but older fingerprints cannot
silently resume under changed code. Config and remaining model budgets are restored.

First Ctrl-C requests controlled closure; a second forces interruption. After an
unresolved request, resume the same run instead of starting a fresh one. Exit 0
means all selected cases have results; exit 2 means incomplete/error. Review the
report and journal. Simulator pickle files are private local state; never import
untrusted ones. Machine/power/network failure and provider outages cannot be
eliminated by the harness; keep the supervisor running on the final machine.

What to hand in for the Tacto track, and how the pitch works. Deadline: **Sunday 12:00 on ehl.gg**.

## What to submit

1. **Your repo:** the agent and a README that says how to run it (setup, the environment variables it

3. **Slides** for the pitch. The top 10 present them from 13:00.

Keep every key out of the repo: no `.env`, no LLM key, no arena key.

## At 12:00 your agent is already running

The code freeze and the Live Final start together, so start your agent before 12:00 and leave it
running:

```bash
uv run arena run --set final --agent llm --parallel 10
```

- `uv run arena me` answers with your team: the key works.

- The runner is started and logs to a file; the laptop is on power and does not sleep.

# learner: negotiation with cautious learning inside one run

Code values terms and validates decisions; an optional model interprets the
supplier's messages and writes emails. LangGraph orchestrates each decision,
with an equivalent sequential fallback.

```text
prepare: dossier + claim catalogue
decide:  observe -> route -> close -> return acceptance immediately
                         -> diverse menu -> model or deterministic choice -> critic
result:  persist Arena result -> background reflection
```

## Decisions and evidence

Every term sheet in the supplier's latest message is valued, but only the
standing (first) sheet can be accepted: the Arena rejects an alternative's ID.
A cheaper alternative is mirrored back as our own sheet, which the supplier
answers with "agreed". Older sheets are not accepted. The ledger, offer builder and last-ask comparison share the
same valuation function. Known buyer costs and the estimated relationship
penalty are exposed separately. Supplier costs, financing and effort remain
assumptions; the public data cannot reveal the Arena's hidden economics. The
generic harness fallback evaluates known costs when it has no supplier model.

The packages of one round cost us within 0.3 % of each other and differ only
in what the supplier gets, because a supplier takes whichever package is
dearest for us. A lever the supplier has insisted on is repriced to the same
cost for us (an index clause comes with a lower base price). Code sizes every
step: we always move (a share of the remaining gap, more when the supplier
moved, most in the end game) and never jump to its offer; the model chooses
among equally priced packages, arguments and wording. Repeated counteroffers and
verbatim, model-interpreted statements create preferences with source evidence.
These preferences rank packages; they are distinct from binding terms and
must-haves. The model can propose allowed nonprice terms. Code computes their
price, checks cost and validates the resulting sheet. A generic should-cost
estimate cannot override an observed supplier price as a hard floor; an
own-plant estimate is calibrated and capped at the margin the opening quote
must carry. The first ask is ambitious but bounded: below the standing price,
at or below today's price in increases and renewals, below the cheapest rival
bid in an RFQ, never below the point where squeezing a relationship supplier
costs more than it saves.

The concession horizon uses actual remaining moves and wave time. There is no
practice-specific four-round cap. Breakdown questions are tracked as asked,
answered or declined, including requests in model-written prose.

## Learning and isolation

`services.history()` supplies only the owning run's confirmed results, tagged
with its run ID. Workers do not discover journals by scanning directories.
Each experiment keeps its configuration, state, attachments, model budget and
results in a separate journal. Source fingerprints include agent helpers and
dependency files, so changing these prevents an old run from resuming silently.

A single outcome creates a hypothesis, not a policy adjustment. Behavioural
changes require at least three distinct cases; scopes spanning suppliers also
require two distinct suppliers. Repeated rounds and overlapping archetypes do
not multiply support. Conflicting anchor evidence reduces confidence. Anchor
adjustments are bounded to ±10%. A final score and an LLM's retrospective
judgment do not establish which claim caused a concession; entire claim kinds
are never blocked by this mechanism.

The engine persists a confirmed result before invoking optional `on_result`.
Deterministic diagnostics are available to subsequent cases immediately.
Optional model reflection skips busy capacity and never delays acceptance.
Asynchronous completion order can still affect which confirmed cases are
available to the next decision; run isolation does not imply identical outcomes.

# Fake It Till You Make It: buyer agent for the Tacto Negotiation Arena

Our entry for the Tacto track at the EHL Grand Finale 2026. The agent, `learner`, buys parts for
Hollerau Pumpenwerke. It negotiates with several suppliers at once by e-mail and term sheets.
**Code makes every money decision**: what each offer costs us, how far we move, and when we accept or
walk away. A language model reads the suppliers' replies and writes our e-mails, and it can only choose
from offers and arguments that code has already priced and checked.

> **Final commit:** the full SHA is in our ehl.gg submission. The final runs exactly that commit, and
> `--commit` refuses to start if the checkout differs.

## Run it

You need Python 3.12 and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/). Every command runs from `starter-kit/`.

```bash
cd starter-kit
uv sync --frozen --extra sim --group dev

# Local simulator: no keys, no network, no model
uv run --frozen arena-harness run --config configs/learner.toml
```

### Environment variables

The harness reads these from the environment. It does not load `.env`, and the repo contains no keys.

| Variable | Needed for | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `ARENA_API_KEY` | practice and final | The team key from arena.tacto.ai |
| `LLM_API_KEY` | practice and final | OpenAI key; the model is set in `configs/learner_final.toml` |
| `ARENA_URL` | optional | Defaults to `https://arena.tacto.ai` |

### Live Final

```bash
cd starter-kit
uv run --frozen arena-harness doctor --profile final --config configs/learner_final.toml
caffeinate -dimsu uv run --frozen arena-harness run --profile final --config configs/learner_final.toml \
  --allow-arena --allow-model --commit "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" 2>&1 | tee ../.runs/final.log
# Only if the supervisor itself died:  uv run --frozen arena-harness resume RUN_ID
```

The runner waits for each of the five waves and plays up to ten cases in parallel inside the 8-minute
cap. It journals every request, so a restart resumes the same run without sending anything twice. It
never reads the leaderboard, events or results. The engine refuses to arm the final unless the Sunday
release is in `data/release-sunday/`.

## How the agent negotiates

```text
prepare  dossier per supplier  ->  claim catalogue (checked data arguments)
decide   read replies -> value every sheet -> close? (accept / walk)
                                            -> otherwise: equally priced packages -> model picks + writes -> critic
```

1. **Prepares from the data.** For each supplier it builds a dossier from the SQLite package and the
   Sunday release: news, letters, call notes, scorecards, past negotiations, payment history and
   should-cost. Keyword rules tag the supplier's situation, for example *cash short*, *price list
   frozen*, *hedged forward*, *sold out* or *spare capacity*. A newer piece of news can end an older
   tag, for example "supply back to normal" after a chip shortage. Each tag sets which levers are
   cheap for us to give and what the supplier values, such as earlier payment for a cash-short
   supplier or a longer contract for one with idle capacity.
2. **Builds arguments that pass the arena's check.** Index falls, scorecards, rival quotes and forecast
   growth become claims whose figures are computed in code and cite their fact IDs. Each message
   carries at most three claims, and no ID is cited twice.
3. **Decides what to offer.** It values every term sheet through the full cost model, covering price,
   payment terms, Incoterm, lead time, contract length and index clauses. Each round it offers two or
   three packages that cost us the same and differ only in what the supplier gets, so they reveal what
   the supplier values. The first ask is ambitious but bounded: below today's price, below the
   cheapest rival bid, and never below the supplier's own should-cost range. After that we always
   concede a share of the remaining gap, and never jump straight to the supplier's number.
4. **Closes or walks.** An acceptable agreement or final offer is held as our fallback while a rival
   can still beat it, then accepted. A final offer is pushed only when the supplier walking would cost
   us nothing. We walk when the last offer is worse than our alternative. When wave time or moves run
   out, we accept the cheapest acceptable offer. The model never makes this decision.
